text: 6:40 a.m. The company website has been down for forty minutes, and the on-call engineer keeps sending nothing but a fire emoji. Join the call straight from the bathroom?
right: Dive into the call in a towel

text: The majority shareholder heard about the app outage from the news before hearing it from you. His message: “So I have to read the papers to know what’s going on in my own company?”
The CTO suggests rolling back yesterday’s release — which kills the new feature you proudly unveiled to the press yesterday. Roll back?
left: Roll back and eat the shame

text: A billing glitch has the call center taking 300 calls an hour since morning. The shift lead is begging for reinforcements from the office. Send in middle management?
The giant lobby screen showing service uptime is proudly glowing 94.2% today. Guests for the investor breakfast are walking right past it. Switch it off?
Morning call from the warehouse: after an update, the sorting robot is arranging parcels alphabetically by the couriers’ last names. Stop the conveyor for half a day?
The press office asks what to call the outage in the official statement: “maintenance” or, honestly, “a failure.” Journalists are already using the word “collapse.”
Your alarm says 5:30, and your phone shows 47 missed calls. The payment gateway went down overnight and nobody dared wake you. Scold the on-call team?
At the morning meeting it turns out the backup data center has been paid for three years and never once tested. Today it finally has to be switched on. Tell the board?
Your main parts supplier says the truck is stuck at the border and the line will stop by lunch. Emergency air freight costs triple. Pay up?
right: Stop the line for a day

text: The reception coffee machine dies on the very day the quality inspectors visit. The secretary offers to run to the café for twenty cappuccinos. Allow it?
The CFO is tallying losses from last night’s outage and wants to postpone quarterly bonuses. The engineers heroically fixed everything all night. Your call?
Since 7 a.m. the exec chat has been arguing whose fault the outage is: IT, product, or marketing, who “overpromised.” Step in?
After the outage, the website support bot answers every customer with one line: “Don’t worry, everything’s under control, probably.” Turn it off?
right: Keep it, it’s kind of cute

text: The server crash killed the electronic badges. Two hundred employees are queuing at the turnstiles, and security asks permission to let people in by ID. What do you do?
The IT director asks for one thing at the meeting: “Please stop asking every five minutes when it’ll be fixed.” You’ve already asked nine times. Hold back?
Your biggest client demands compensation for four hours of downtime — equal to a full year’s contract. Legal says the contract entitles them to a twentieth of that. Haggle?
The board wants a written report on the outage’s causes by 3 p.m. Engineers will know the cause by evening, at best. What do you write?
The product manager wants to turn the outage into a promo: “We went down, you get 20% off!” Marketing loves it, finance is horrified. Approve it?
While you’re at lunch, the outage hits the top of the news. Most-liked comment: “Do they even have a CEO?” Finish your soup?
right: Ditch the soup, go on air

text: The chief engineer found the cause: a bug in code he himself wrote five years ago. He asks you not to name him at the post-mortem. Agree?
Your packaging supplier went bankrupt; in a week there’ll be nothing to pack products in. Logistics found a replacement: bright pink boxes. Take them?
Quality control found a defective batch that’s already on store shelves. Announce a recall now, or first assess the scale?
An intern single-handedly found the source of the outage while the seniors hunted for someone to blame. He’s shy and asks not to be praised publicly. Reward him?
left: Reward him in front of all

text: An industry site publishes “Five Signs a Company Is on Its Last Legs.” Four of the five are lifted straight from yesterday’s outage. Respond?
Your distribution partner offers to take over your logistics for a while, “as a friend.” The fine print: five-year exclusivity. Sign?
The plant stopped because of a broken part made in only one country. A mechanic offers to machine a copy in his brother-in-law’s garage. Risk it?
right: Wait three weeks for the real one

text: The security specialist goes pale: the customer address database has been posted on a forum. The law requires notifying customers. Email all 400,000 today?
The breach investigation shows the database password was “Admin2019,” written on a sticky note on a monitor. Your monitor. How do you present this at the review?
Legal advises against apologizing for the breach in the public statement: an apology could be used in court. The PR lead says without one you’ll be eaten alive. Who do you listen to?
Your assistant books the fifth crisis meeting of the day. The previous four mostly discussed when to meet again. Cancel the fifth?
The anonymous thieves who stole the database send a ransom demand, politely signed “Kind regards.” Security says don’t reply. The board wants to “make a deal.” Your decision?
A retail chain threatens to pull your products over missed deliveries. You could divert stock from another region that needs it just as badly. Reallocate?
The chief accountant reminds you: because of the payment system crash, salaries won’t go out today. Staff don’t know yet. Announce now or hope for a miracle by evening?
9 p.m. The service is finally back up. The on-call team suggests celebrating with pizza at the office. The board expects your final report by morning. Who are you with tonight?
A board member calls at 10:30 p.m. asking whether it’s time to “refresh” IT leadership after the outage. The IT director is your longtime ally. Your answer?
At dinner your schoolboy son asks: “Is that your company’s website everyone’s joking about?” He shows you the jokes on his phone. Explain or laugh?
By evening, support has answered 11,000 complaints and asks for tomorrow off for the whole shift. Tomorrow is forecast to be even worse. Let them go?
The evening news wants you live at 9 p.m. about the outage. You’ve been on your feet since dawn in a shirt with a coffee stain. Agree?
Your inner voice whispers that the outage could have been prevented if, six months ago, you’d signed the budget for backups instead of the new lounge. Talk it over?
right: Tell the voice to shut up

text: Late evening. The night shift supervisor says restarting the line needs your personal order and a wet-ink signature. The office is an hour away. Go?
Your deputy suggests giving every customer a $15 promo code as an apology. It’ll fix the reviews and empty the marketing budget. Do it?
Your country-house neighbor saw you on the news and drops by with homemade kvass “for moral support” — then stays to tell you about his own work disaster back in 1998.
The internal outage review committee wants to interview everyone involved before the weekend. That’s 60 people and two evenings. Speed it up?
A minority shareholder posts an evening video, “What’s going on with this company?”, and racks up 40,000 views. Reply with your own video?
left: Film a reply in the kitchen

text: Overnight the warehouse fire alarm went off: the smoke came from the guard’s toaster. But the goods are already soaked in foam. Tell customers about delays?
Your business partner invites you for drinks tonight “to forget this day.” Tomorrow at 8 a.m. you meet the regulator about the outage. Go?
Security wants all 3,000 employees to change passwords by morning after the breach. Half will forget the new one by lunch. Do it?
Your co-founder’s wife messages you privately: he hasn’t slept in three days because of the outage and won’t answer his phone. She asks you to send him home. Step in?
At day’s end the chief engineer brings a plan to “rebuild the whole architecture over the weekend.” Eyes blazing, plan on a napkin. Give your blessing?
The night guard found the server room wide open, the key hanging on a nail under a sign reading “Server room key.” Handle it yourself?
Checking email before bed: a message from the regulator titled “Questions about the incident,” marked urgent. Open it now?
The fund that owns 30% of the company offers to send “their crisis manager” to help. He’d sit in your office. Accept?
7:05 a.m. A journalist with a mic waits outside your building: “Is it true the company is for sale?” You’re in sweatpants holding a trash bag. Stop?
The press secretary brings the morning roundup: 14 articles about you; three call you “charismatic,” one calls you “gloomy.” Get upset over the one?
A business paper wants a cover photo for its “Top 50 Leaders” ranking. The photographer arrives at 8 a.m. and wants you “in your natural habitat” — in the kitchen with porridge.
A trade magazine editor wants your column “on leadership” by 10 a.m. You promised it two weeks ago and successfully forgot. Write it yourself?
A reporter calls to check a quote: supposedly you said “Competitors don’t scare us, they amuse us.” You said “don’t scare us.” Insist on a fix?
Live morning radio. Instead of the economy, the host asks what you had for breakfast. You had yesterday’s pizza. Confess?
A popular business blogger wants an interview, but only “walk-and-talk” style at 6 a.m. on the waterfront while he jogs. Agree?
The press office forgot to mention that a press release went out quoting you on a “breakthrough innovation.” You’re seeing it for the first time and have no idea which innovation. Now what?
In the morning paper, your photo is captioned with the name of your rival’s CEO. His photo has yours. Call the editors?
right: Call the rival for a laugh

text: The PR director pitches a new strategy: “be closer to the people” — starting with a personal blog you post to every morning. Try it?
A TV channel sends interview questions in advance. Question seven: “Why are your employees complaining en masse on social media?” This is the first you’ve heard of it.
Your assistant has written you an interview “backstory”: you wake at five, read a book a day, and don’t drink coffee. All false except “wake.” Approve?
An industry portal sends your interview for approval. The journalist “lightly edited” your answers — you now sound like a symbolist poet. Edit it?
At a press event, the photographer asks you to “smile in a businesslike way and gaze into the future.” You don’t know where it is. How many more takes can you stand?
A journalist you went to university with asks for an exclusive on the merger. The deal isn’t closed yet. Friendship versus protocol.
The communications director thinks you need media training: “You say ‘like’ way too often.” Sessions at 7 a.m., three weeks straight. Sign up?
An investigative reporter wants comment on procurement documents from five years ago, when your predecessor ran the company. Comment?
At a press conference, a journalist asks a question that lasts four minutes and never ends in a question mark. Everyone awaits your reaction.
The press office wants approval for a rebuttal to an article only 200 people have read. After the rebuttal, thousands will read it. Publish?
A talk show host invites you to debate your rival’s CEO in the studio. Last time, the rival brought charts on poster board. Go?
Over lunch, the editor-in-chief of a major outlet mentions that “the story about your layoffs” may or may not run. A hint about buying ads?
A PR intern accidentally emailed every outlet a draft release with the note “need to fudge the numbers here.” The phone won’t stop ringing. How do you react?
A journalist suggests chatting “off the record” about rumors of your departure. Experience says “off the record” lasts until the article comes out. Talk?
Mid-interview recording, your phone rings. It’s the board. The camera is rolling, the journalist watches with interest. Answer?
The press secretary learns you gave an unapproved interview after just “getting chatty in the elevator.” It’s already aired. She’s furious. Apologize?
A media group wants to make a documentary about the company. The film crew would live in the office for two weeks. Staff are already nervous.
A fact-checker reviewing your interview finds that “300% growth” was actually 30%. You misspoke. The outlet asks how to correct it.
A columnist calls your new office an “aquarium of vanity.” Employees printed the column and pinned it by the water cooler. Take it down?
A journalist asks to see the factory. The floor manager whispers that today’s a bad day: line three is in a state of “temporary creative chaos.” Let the press in?
The media analyst reports: press mentions are up 40%. Though 38% of them are about the outage. How do you pitch this to the board?
A PR agency offers, for a hefty sum, a “guaranteed spot in the top business news.” Their methods are secret. Sign?
The press office compiled an “enemies folder”: journalists who wrote badly about you. Forty names. They suggest never inviting them to events again.
The interviewer asks you to name the three biggest mistakes of your career. The first two come easily; the third is too recent and involves the board.
A reporter mixed things up and came to interview you instead of your namesake — the chef at the restaurant downstairs. The questions are about pizza dough. Answer?
On live evening TV, the host reads out an angry letter from a former employee of yours. You have to respond live.
10 p.m. A journalist writes: “The story runs tomorrow, you have an hour to comment.” The story is unknown, the gist undisclosed. Respond?
You’re invited onto the evening podcast “Business, Honestly.” Format: three hours, no script, hosted by former stand-up comics. Go?
At 11 p.m. the press secretary sends edits to tomorrow’s statement. 120 of them, including changing “esteemed” to “dear.” Review them now?
A journalist sends the piece for approval: all accurate, but your portrait is shot from the least flattering angle imaginable. Ask for a swap?
Your daughter shows you a viral video: you, at a conference, expressively scratching your nose during someone else’s talk. Her classmates have already made stickers of it.
The evening paper runs the headline “CEO Admits Failure.” In the interview you said: “I admit failure would have been possible.” Complain?
Your PR adviser, a former journalist, suggests leaking competitor news to distract from your scandal. Tempting.
An entertainment show host invites you to a celebrity-CEO cooking contest. Airs Saturday night. You can’t fry an egg.
The overnight media digest: a glowing article about you, but it mentions “your modesty” thirty times. Staff are already being ironic. How do you react?
The press tour is dragging on: at 8 p.m. the journalists want to “continue informally” at the company’s expense. There’s no budget for this.
Before publishing, a journalist asks for “literally five more clarifications.” This is the fifth round and the fifth “literally.” Your patience is running out.
right: Refer her to the press office

text: The press office is thrilled: you’re invited onto the cover of a style magazine. The shoot is at 9 p.m. in an unusual suit in “warm terracotta.” Agree?
Late in the evening, your secretary reports five journalists staking out the main entrance. There’s a service exit through the parking garage. Which way out?
8:10 a.m. The forum organizer calls: your talk moved from 3 p.m. to 9 a.m. because “the guest of honor is running late.” Your slides aren’t ready. Go on anyway?
The speechwriter sent your conference opening speech. It says “synergy” 14 times and quotes a philosopher you’ve never read. Edit it?
At sound check, the engineer asks you to say something into the mic. You say “testing, testing,” and the whole hall — already full of guests — hears it. Carry on?
left: Crack a joke into the mic

text: The host introduces you as “the person who led the company out of crisis.” You actually led it into one — just last month. Correct him?
The teleprompter freezes two minutes into your speech. 800 people in the hall. The last line on screen: “And that is why we.”
The panel moderator asks everyone to “describe the industry’s future in one word.” Your neighbors already said “digital,” “people,” and “sustainability.”
Right before going on stage, you discover a dry-cleaning tag dangling from your jacket. No time to rip it off — they’re announcing you. Go out like that?
Your public speaking coach advises you to “shout loudly in an empty room” before going on. There are no empty rooms, just a bathroom with an echo.
At the morning session, the speaker before you shows slides suspiciously similar to your upcoming presentation. He’s on your own team.
left: Rework your talk on the fly

text: Your assistant reminds you that today you’re speaking at three conferences in three corners of the city. The taxi is already stuck in traffic on the first leg.
right: Take the subway to all three

text: A morning email: you’ve been nominated for “Leader of the Year.” To compete, you must record a video “about your values” by noon.
A conference organizer asks you to speak for free — “but the audience will be great.” The audience: eight students and a coffee break.
The simultaneous interpreter asks for your speech in advance: yesterday you joked on stage and he translated the joke as “a threat.” Send it?
The press office wants you to announce the new strategy at the conference. The board approves the strategy on Thursday. The conference is Wednesday.
Your alarm didn’t go off, and you’re opening the industry congress at 9:00. The venue is 40 minutes away; it’s 8:45. Call your deputy?
right: Open via video from the taxi

text: The corporate event director wants you to ride on stage on an electric unicycle — “to show drive.” You’ve never ridden one.
After your talk, a hand goes up: “How do you sleep at night after the layoffs?” The cameras swing toward you.
The moderator keeps interrupting and handing the floor to your competitor. You’ve started “Allow me to add” three times. Insist?
After your talk, an attendee comes up and says your slide 12 is an exact copy of his article from five years ago. He’s right.
Mid-talk, a notification from your personal messenger pops up on the big screen: “Buy bread and don’t forget the cat.” The hall laughs.
At the coffee break, five startup founders surround you with pitches. Each needs “literally a minute.” Your coffee’s going cold; the next session is in ten minutes.
The organizers offer you a seat on the main stage next to the head of a major holding. In exchange: a sponsorship fee from the marketing budget.
At a public debate, your opponent shows a chart of your company plunging. You notice the chart’s axis is upside down. Point it out?
Your lapel mic came unstuck and slid down your collar. You keep talking, but now you sound like you’re in a barrel. Stop and fix it?
The organizers ask you to cut your talk from 30 minutes to 7: “The main sponsor is late, we need to free up time.” How do you cut it?
You’re invited to speak at an international conference. In English — which you last spoke at a student summer job.
After a university lecture, a student asks how much you earn. The hall freezes. The professor pretends to be busy with a laptop.
On a panel, your own marketing director publicly disagrees with you. The moderator perks up: “Now this is interesting!”
You’re invited to chair a startup competition jury. 40 pitches in a day, three minutes each, scores on the spot. Accept the honor?
The slide clicker dies. An assistant in the hall advances slides when you say “next” — but always skips two ahead.
You’re hosting a client webinar, but the stream accidentally shows your assistant’s screen instead of yours — with a chat reading “he’s driving me crazy.”
At the trade show, your booth is right next to the restrooms. Foot traffic is huge, but the marketing value is questionable. Ask to be moved?
The designer sent the final deck: beautiful, but every number “flies in” over a second and a half. There are 200 numbers.
At the post-conference lunch, you’re seated next to an investor who walked out on you a year ago, slamming the door. He waves his fork at you.
The post-conference gala dinner. You’re asked to give a toast “on behalf of the industry.” It must be witty, short, and offend none of the 300 guests.
The organizers posted your talk online. First comment: “Never actually answered the question.” Second: “But what a tie.” Staff are already watching.
The industry forum afterparty: all the industry’s top brass are heading to karaoke. Rumor has it that’s where all the big deals get made.
After the conference, it turns out the hotel gave your room to another attendee. All that’s left is a suite on the company dime or a cot in a colleague’s room.
At home, your family is asked to hear a rehearsal of tomorrow’s speech. After two minutes the cat leaves; after five, so does your partner.
Late at night the organizers write: “Can you replace a sick speaker tomorrow at 8 a.m.? Topic: quantum computing.” Your topic is dairy products.
The evening brings the forum’s speaker ranking: you’re 23rd out of 25. Below you: a broken mic and a talk with a typo in its title.
Your deputy spoke at the evening session in your place and got a standing ovation. The board is already congratulating him in the group chat.
After the conference, you’re stuck at the airport with a delayed flight. You can spend the night working in the lounge or at a hotel near the airport.
In your jacket pocket you find a note someone slipped you after your talk: “Your speech changed my life. Please hire me.” Reply?
An industry executive club invites you to join. The fee is hefty, meetings are monthly evenings, and the club blazer is mandatory.
The interns ask you to speak at their graduation. You prepared an inspiring speech; they expect you to sing the company anthem with them.
In the feedback forms, 90% rate your talk “excellent,” but one person wrote “boring as a tax report.” All evening, that one is all you can think about.
In the evening you record a podcast for the internal portal. Take six: you say “like” again. The sound engineer sighs wearily.
7:20 a.m. Overnight the official company account posted a Monday meme with “Monday” misspelled. It already has 3,000 comments. Delete it?
The social media manager confesses he accidentally liked a competitor’s post “Why We’re the Best” from the company account yesterday. People noticed. What do we say?
An employee made a clip, “A Day in Our Office,” showing the coffee machine spitting and the printer on fire. It hit a million views. Punish him?
Since morning, a hashtag with your company’s name and the word “boycott” is trending. Even the press office doesn’t know why yet. What do you do?
Someone dug up your ten-year-old post calling your future industry “boring, for losers.” It’s spreading fast.
The community manager answered angry comments all night and, judging by screenshots, by 3 a.m. was seriously arguing with customers. What do you do?
Your deputy posted a story with a photo from a meeting. In the background: a whiteboard reading “Layoff plan, do not show.” It’s been up for 7 hours.
A blogger with a million followers posted a review of your product titled “Never Buy This.” The reason: the wrong button on the packaging. Call him?
The press office suggests starting a personal account for you to post motivational quotes. An intern will write the quotes.
Your morning feed shows an employee in company uniform dancing on the hood of a company car. The video is taking off; customers love it.
The monitoring system wakes you: “Sharp spike in negativity.” Turns out people are just confusing your company with a pizzeria of the same name.
A PR agency offers to “drown out the negativity” with a stream of positive reviews from “real users” they’ll find themselves. The price is reasonable.
Your former sales director published a long post, “Why I Left.” No names, but everyone knows. It’s getting shared widely.
The ad specialist launched a campaign overnight, and it’s showing under news of your own outage: “Our service never lets you down!” Stop the campaign?
A meme is going around with your face from yesterday’s interview captioned “When they tell you on Friday you’re working Saturday.” Staff are making it their wallpaper.
right: Ask for it to be removed

text: The sales team’s internal chat leaked: customers are referred to as “guinea pigs.” Screenshots are everywhere. Who gets fired?
A video blogger shows up at your office unannounced to film a “company inspection,” asking security “who’s in charge here.”
The social team wants to launch a “Dance with the CEO” challenge. You’d need to film 15 seconds of dancing in the lobby. They promise massive reach.
People online note that everyone in the company’s ads is a stock-photo model, while real employees are “hiding.” Your response?
Marketing wants to answer a competitor’s criticism with a cheeky “At least we don’t...” post. It’s funny, but the lawyers wince. Publish?
Customers on social media demand that “the CEO answer personally.” There are 2,000 complaints. Answer them?
Someone screenshots your message from the private execs’ chat: “Well, let them quit then.” It’s out of context but sounds awful.
An employee runs a popular blog about work and trashes management, though without names. Many recognize you as “the big boss.” Talk to him?
A bot shows up in the comments under your new post, replying to everything with “so when are you raising salaries?” The bot seems suspiciously human.
An influencer with a dodgy reputation wants to be your brand’s “ambassador” for free. He’s already posted a photo with your product captioned “my sponsor.”
The new ad campaign is divisive: half think the slogan is genius, half think it’s baffling. The board is split too.
The company ran a social media poll to name a new product. The trolls’ entry won: “Producty McProductface.” Accept it?
The agency proposes deleting negative comments under the company’s posts. There’s less negativity now, but those who noticed are writing even more about censorship.
Slides from your internal “Strategy 2030” presentation are now public. Most popular: the slide with a kitten you used to fill an empty spot.
Someone made a fake account in your name and replies to everyone with “I’ll handle it personally.” The fake has more followers than you.
The press office asks you to personally answer questions in the corporate channel on Fridays. First Friday’s question: “Why is your car worth more than my apartment?”
The marketing director suggests publicly admitting a product flopped: “We got it wrong, and here’s why.” The board fears it’ll hit the stock price.
The company’s anniversary video is shot in “we’re one big family” style. In the comments, ex-employees recall how the “family” didn’t pay overtime.
During the annual meeting livestream, pranksters invade the chat and every word you say gets a clown emoji. There’s no moderator.
In the evening an employee posts “My CEO is the best” with a photo of you asleep on the meeting room couch after an all-nighter. It goes viral.
11 p.m. An old photo surfaces in your feed: you in a pirate costume at a company party in front of the logo. Caption: “This is who decides the fate of 3,000 people.”
The social media manager sent the week’s post plan. Friday’s has an emoji that teens now use to mean something indecent. Remove it?
Your teenager says they saw people online calling your company “boring.” They offer to “level up” its social media themselves.
An anonymous channel, “Industry Insiders,” claims you’re about to leave. You weren’t, but by evening three headhunters have called.
In the evening you see a review on an employer-rating site: “The CEO is nice but never listens.” 300 likes.
You accidentally posted a photo of your dinner on the corporate account instead of the quarterly results. Noticed an hour later.
Overnight an online debate erupts: your logo supposedly resembles that of some obscure band. The logo designer is on standby.
The board wants a video apology for the ad scandal. Take fifteen, and your voice still sounds “insincere.”
Your PR adviser asks you not to leave the house unless necessary: your face has been in memes for a week. But you have a parent-teacher meeting.
The corporate channel posts your message at 11:30 p.m.: “Have a great weekend, everyone.” Staff respond with the “sleeping face” reaction.
The PR lead calls: the influencer you turned down for an ad deal filmed a video, “How the CEO Humiliated Me.” It goes up tomorrow morning.
Your inner voice suggests deleting all your social media tonight so you’ll never land in a scandal again. Your finger is hovering over the button.
8 a.m. Security reports three inspectors with folders in the lobby — a surprise inspection. You’re stuck in traffic, your office is a mess, and your deputy is on vacation. What now?
The fire inspector starts with your office and immediately finds an extension cord plugged into an extension cord plugged into another extension cord.
Health inspectors arrive at the plant at 7 a.m. The shift supervisor asks you to hold them at the gate for 15 minutes, “literally just to tidy up.” Stall them?
First thing in the morning, the chief accountant reports that the tax office wants five years of documents within ten days. Year three’s archive is in the basement — which flooded.
The regulator sends new reporting requirements: 140 pages, effective in a month. The CFO is panicking. Hire consultants?
The inspector asks for a private office for three weeks. The only free one is your favorite meeting room with a park view.
Your secretary whispers that “some serious man from the oversight agency” is here and already photographing the fire extinguishers in the hall. Go out yourself?
The quality director asks to postpone the certification audit: “We’re 80% ready.” Postponing costs money; failing costs more.
The labor inspector wants to talk to rank-and-file staff with no managers present. You know the installers have a pile of grievances.
Inspectors notice suspiciously colorful smoke coming from the boiler house chimney. The boiler house chief insists it’s “just morning mist.”
The regulator’s lab took product samples. Results in a week. The production head suggests holding the batch until then. Your call.
The inspection commission demands every order from the past three years by 10 a.m., on paper and bound. You went paperless two years ago.
The inspector finds your signature on an order you definitely never signed. It looks very much like yours. Someone clearly made an effort.
The external auditor arrives at 8 a.m. and asks for a “plain human explanation of revenue.” The CFO has been explaining it inhumanly for three days.
Your core business license expires in a week. The renewal papers went in, but the company name has a typo — one letter. Refile?
A building inspector demands you demolish an annex built ten years ago as a smoking area. It’s now the board’s meeting room.
The inspector asks to see the safety briefing log. It exists, but for six months it’s been signed by someone named “Smith-Test.”
The agency fined you for the wrong font on a label. The amount is small, but an appeal takes a month and is winnable. Pay?
During the inspection, the inspector asks why there’s no soap in the staff restroom. There is soap — in the facilities manager’s office, “just in case.”
The CFO suggests hiring tax consultants who “know people at the tax office.” You don’t like the word “know.”
The inspector wants to climb onto the factory roof to check the railings. The roof key is lost. A mechanic offers a ladder that itself needs inspecting.
The antitrust agency is curious about your joint project with a competitor. The project: a joint company soccer tournament. Explain?
The inspector found that the fire extinguisher in your reception is being used as a doorstop. The secretary swears it still works.
Auditors found that procurement bought 400 office chairs for a department of 40. The chairs are sitting in a hangar. Explain to the board?
right: Find a use for the chairs

text: A government agency wants a form filled out. Mandatory field: “hours worked by the third-floor cleaner in 2021.” Where would you even get that?
The tax inspector summons you personally for a chat. Legal says say nothing, accounting says explain everything. The board demands you “just sort it out.”
The inspection drags on: for three weeks the inspectors have eaten free in your cafeteria, and the cook has started making them a special menu. Stop it?
left: Put them on the regular menu

text: You’ve been ordered to build a wheelchair ramp at the service entrance within a month. The contractor says he needs two. Hire a second one?
At an industry meeting, the regulator asks your experts to help draft new rules. An honor — but it’s five people for six months.
Legal brings an inspection-prep plan: 30 points, including “teach everyone to say ‘that’s not my area.’” Approve it?
During an inspection, the metrologist finds all the warehouse scales are off by 50 grams — in the customers’ favor. You’ve been losing money for three years.
The certification board wants the product tested at minus 40. The nearest freezer belongs to the meatpacking plant next door.
left: Strike a deal with the meat plant

text: Evening. The inspector lingers and hints that “the inspection could wrap up faster if...” He doesn’t finish the sentence and looks at you expectantly.
At 7:30 p.m. you’re handed a 70-page inspection report. It must be signed by morning; objections within three days. Read it tonight?
The board chair calls in the evening: “Heard you have an inspection. I trust we won’t have to blush at the shareholder meeting?” Give details?
In the evening, an employee comes to confess: for two years he’s been signing the safety logs for everyone because “it’s faster.” The inspection is tomorrow.
Accounting is working late on the tax request. The chief accountant asks you to order them food and “sit with us for moral support.”
In the evening you discover the quarterly regulator report was sent with an empty table. Deadline: midnight. It’s 11:40 p.m.
right: Send it in the morning with a note

text: At home, a candlelit anniversary dinner awaits. In your inbox: a letter from the regulator marked “response required today.”
Internal audit brings an evening report: the company has 47 different rules for running meetings, and they contradict each other. Cut it to one?
The night watchman calls: the inspector left a folder marked “Preliminary findings” in the meeting room. It’s lying open. Take a peek?
Late evening notification: the company is on next year’s scheduled inspection plan. All twelve months. Tell the team?
The lawyers stay late preparing objections to the report. One asks you to personally check the word “willful” — it has to be contested by midnight.
The board chair wants a plan by morning on “how to never get inspected again.” No such plan exists in nature.
8:30 a.m. A courier hands you, personally, a lawsuit from a former partner for an amount equal to annual revenue. You have to sign for it right there in the elevator.
General counsel reports the company won the case. But the win is $1 in symbolic damages, and legal fees hit $100,000. Celebrate?
Legal advises you not to take calls from the former director who sued you. He calls every morning just to ask how you’re doing.
In your mailbox: a court summons in your name. The hearing is today at 10:00. The letter apparently took three weeks to arrive. Go?
Your outside law firm sent its monthly bill. The line item “Reflections on strategy” is billed at 60 hours. Dispute it?
A patent attorney warns your new product may infringe a competitor’s patent. Launch is in a week. Postpone?
A customer sues: your product’s manual “doesn’t warn against using it in a swimming pool.” The product is an office chair.
Legal wants to rewrite all client contracts within a month to “plug the holes.” Sales is wailing that clients will flee.
You’re asked to testify in a former supplier’s case. The hearing is at 9 a.m. — the same day as the board meeting.
A legal assistant accidentally sent the opposing side internal emails labeled “our weak points.” What now?
A former employee sues to be reinstated. By now his position has been eliminated and his desk given to a printer.
Legal asks you to approve a “delay strategy”: five motions to postpone so the plaintiff gets tired. Legal, but it sounds ugly.
A competitor sued, claiming your slogan “Simply Better” is misleading. The lawyers suggest changing it to “Simply Good.”
A mediator offers to settle your dispute with a supplier. Condition: you personally call their CEO and apologize. Their CEO is your old classmate.
In court, the judge rebukes you over your phone. A minute later it rings again: the board. For the third time.
A law firm partner suggests filing a countersuit “for balance.” Odds of winning are slim, but the other side will get nervous.
The other side offers a settlement on good terms but demands a public statement that “you were wrong.”
Legal says the defense needs all correspondence from the past three years. Including the “Friday Memes” chat where you joked about a competitor.
Your key witness — a manager — quit the day before the hearing and joined a competitor. He writes politely: “Good luck in court!”
The union threatens a class action over the new remote work rules. The board thinks the rules are fair.
Legal discovered that a key supplier contract ran for ten years without your side’s signature. Both sides honored it. Is that a problem?
A court-appointed expert wants two days of access to the plant. Technically, production can’t be stopped. What now?
A client sent a 47-page complaint. Legal says it boils down to one demand; the rest is emotion and drawings. Read it yourself?
Legal wants a rule: every email to partners gets a legal review. Sales estimates replies will take three days.
During a recess, the opposing lawyer buys you coffee and asks “how your board is feeling.” Keep chatting?
A bailiff has come to seize assets over an old case you thought was closed. He’s already putting a sticker on your coffee machine.
The lawyers suggest moving some assets into a subsidiary “just in case.” Legal, but the board may ask what we’re hiding from.
Customers are preparing a class action because a “Family Pack” of cookies contains eight, and their family has nine people.
General counsel calls at 9 p.m.: “Good news and bad news.” Good: the trial’s postponed. Bad: by a month, and you’ll have to prep all over again.
Legal suggests “quickly” proofreading a 500-page contract with a new investor tonight. Signing is tomorrow at 10 a.m.
Your former business partner, whom you’re suing, invites you to dinner to “talk without lawyers.” The lawyers are dead against it.
At dinner, your kid asks why the TV said your company “got sued.” You didn’t know it was already on the news.
The verdict arrives in the evening: you lost. The lawyers are sure you’ll win on appeal, but the board must be told today. Call?
Your law firm invites you to an evening client reception. Your legal bill this year is so big you probably paid for this party.
left: Go and eat your money’s worth

text: An employee who lost to you at ping-pong at the company party yesterday is now threatening to sue for “psychological pressure.”
The on-duty lawyer wants to answer a supplier’s claim with his trademark sarcasm. The reply is already written and very witty.
Signing a contract in the evening, you notice legal misspelled the company name: “Alpa” instead of “Alpha.” The counterparty is waiting until 8 p.m.
The attorney calls in the evening and asks you to “keep a stone face no matter what” in court. Tomorrow the other side will read out your old joking emails.
The reputation director brings a study: 62% of people don’t know what your company does, and 18% are sure you make furniture. You make yogurt.
The company dropped off the best-employers list. HR proposes fixing it with “immediate changes” — like free fruit on Fridays.
The PR director wants to rename the company to “escape old negativity.” The new name was invented over the weekend: “Neo-Synergetics.”
The morning news praises your company for a charity drive you know nothing about. Turns out logistics organized it on their own. Take the credit?
An agency brings a brand book for your personal brand. It specifies your “signature gesture,” “tone of voice,” and “favorite book.” You haven’t read the book.
Production reports glass fragments found in a batch of children’s juice. The batch is already in 40 stores. Recall everything or just the suspicious boxes?
A retail chain calls at 7:45 a.m.: a shopper found the wrong product in your packaging — shoe polish instead of toothpaste. The video’s already online.
The procurement director reports: due to a storm, the ship with raw materials is going around the continent. Six weeks’ delay. Buy from a pricey local supplier?
This morning it turns out the cloud storage with job applicants’ résumés was open to everyone all summer. A journalist has already found it.
An employee accidentally sent the whole office’s salary list to the all-staff mailing list. 300 people read it in 4 minutes. Recall it?
The agency offers to buy you an entry in the encyclopedia “Outstanding Leaders of Our Era.” Price: a used car. Print run unknown.
The call center reports that after the recall, customers are demanding the recalled product back because “it was tasty.” What do we say?
The sole supplier of a unique part is shutting down. You could buy their entire stock — ten years’ worth. The warehouse would be packed to the ceiling.
Quality wants the press release to say “Defect rate under 0.01%.” You know they only counted one shift out of three. Send it?
A partner coffee chain refuses to sell your product until you “sort out your reputation.” That’s 15% of revenue. Go negotiate?
The press secretary proposes declaring a “year of openness”: every month you meet journalists and answer any question.
At 7 a.m., a major shareholder sends a link to the “Most Hated Brands of the Year” list with one word: “Explain.” You’re 11th.
The contractor admits the factory in your commercial wasn’t yours but someone else’s — “it was prettier.” Their logo is visible in the shot.
Marketing wants to relaunch a product recalled a year ago under a new name. “Nobody will remember,” they promise.
An agency shows you a word cloud of what the internet says about the company. The biggest word: “meh.” They pitch a six-month plan.
A product manager finds 30,000 mugs in the warehouse with the company name misspelled on the logo. They’re already paid for.
Production asks to ship a batch in last year’s packaging because the new design is stuck at customs. Will anyone notice?
The warehouse reports a system glitch sent 2,000 orders to one town where exactly one customer lives. He’s delighted, if a bit puzzled.
Sales wants to use the line “The stars choose us” in ads. There’s one star — the sales director’s distant relative, a karaoke singer.
At a business breakfast, you’re introduced as “the person who nearly sank the company last year.” The host thinks it’s a compliment.
The PR director wants approval to sponsor a kids’ soccer team. The team loses every match 0–10. Your logo would be on their backs.
Quality control found that your “all-natural” product contains artificial colors. You’re only finding out now too. Tell customers?
The packaging supplier raised prices 40% overnight. The alternative: paper packaging that survives three days of humidity.
The ad team wants the slogan recorded in your voice. After five takes, the sound engineer gently asks whether you have a “warmer” voice.
The investigation shows customer data leaked through a lunch-ordering app employees installed themselves. Ban it?
A consumer protection group invites you to an open meeting with unhappy customers. About 200 people and one camera.
The board wants you to “urgently improve the company’s reputation” before the shareholder meeting. It’s in a week. No budget allocated.
Quality control wants to stop the line for a day over a suspected defect. The suspicion is based on a machine making a “weird noise.”
Your deputy wants to start a personal blog, “Diary of a Deputy Director.” The first post is ready: “What’s really going on at our company.”
A container of parts is held at customs: the declaration says “bananas.” The broker insists it’s a “system typo.”
The PR agency wants weekend photos of you in “ordinary life”: on the subway, at the market, with your dog. You don’t have a dog.
On the evening news, the story about your product recall runs right after a story about a heroic firefighter. The contrast doesn’t flatter you.
The quality director is staying late and asks you to sign off on destroying a batch worth $2 million. Disposal starts in the morning.
A board member suggests solving the reputation problem “like grown-ups”: donate to charity and pose with a giant check.
A former colleague texts in the evening: “Saw you on the news. Hang in there, it’ll blow over in a week.” A minute later: “Well, maybe two.”
Support asks permission to close the reviews section on the website tonight until the wave of anger over the recall dies down.
10 p.m. Logistics calls: the shipment is stuck on a mountain pass in a snowstorm, and the driver is writing poems in the chat and says hi.
Your assistant asks you to sign anniversary cards for partners tonight. There are 400, and each signature must be “handwritten” and different.
In response to the bad press, the PR director suggests publishing a memoir, “How I Saved the Company.” A specially hired “literary assistant” would write it.
Your inner voice asks whether it’s time to reread every quote you gave the press this year to figure out where exactly it all went wrong.
On an evening call, minority shareholders demand the marketing director be fired over a failed ad. The ad was your idea.
The recalled batch of cookies is selling online as a “collector’s item” at triple the price. Meanwhile the company is taking losses.
Security reports late at night: the customer data leak seems to be the work of a fired sysadmin. He left a note in the code: “Hi to the CEO.”
At 9 p.m. a supplier offers to fix the delay if you sign a two-year contract at an inflated price. Answer needed by midnight.
A childhood friend writes: “Saw your product got recalled. I’m still eating it, is that okay?” She wants an honest answer.
6:50 a.m. The shift foreman calls: overnight, the packing robot sealed 5,000 empty boxes. They’ve already gone out to distributors. Call them before opening?
The IT director proposes a “drill”: deliberately shutting down the main server during work hours to test the backup. The board is nervous.
A pricing glitch has the company’s online store selling refrigerators for $1 since morning. 800 orders already. Honor them?
The board chair wants a “short crisis summary” every morning at 7:00. Short means “one page, but with charts.”
The service desk is swamped: employees can’t log into email after the password reset. Most common question: “What was my old password?”
The warehouse reports that after moving to a new system, nobody knows where anything is. Shipments have stopped. Rehire the “old” storekeeper?
The chief technologist suggests replacing an expensive ingredient with a cheap substitute “nobody can tell apart.” Quality control could tell from the first spoonful.
After the leak, security wants fingerprint scanners at the entrance. Staff have already nicknamed it “the police station.”
Security reports a picket of five people outside with signs saying “Bring back the old flavor!” They’re polite and brought a thermos.
An industry forum moderator offers you a morning session: “How We Survived the Crisis.” The crisis isn’t over.
By 9 a.m. the press office needs you to choose between two statements: “We regret the inconvenience” and “This is our fault.” Lawyers love the first; people love the second.
A corporate client writes at 7:30 a.m.: “We want to cancel over the data leak. But if your CEO comes in person, we might reconsider.”
A partner factory abroad has closed for a “national holiday” nobody knew about. It lasts nine days. The line is stopping.
An analyst shows that every hour of downtime costs the company an analyst’s annual salary. He gives you a meaningful look.
The board recommends hiring a crisis consultant who bills hourly and loves to say “let’s start with values.”
On the subway, you overhear two passengers discussing your scandal. One says: “I hear the CEO is decent, though.” The other disagrees.
The HR director reports that 30 candidates canceled interviews over the scandal. One wrote: “I’ll wait until things settle down.”
The power company warns that at 10 a.m. the whole district loses power for four hours. The diesel generator hasn’t been tested in three years.
The chief engineer wants money for a monitoring system that warns of outages an hour in advance. There hasn’t been an outage in six months. The board thinks it’s unnecessary.
The new packaging supplier made the boxes a centimeter too small. The product doesn’t fit. A reprint takes two weeks.
A logistics partner offers drone delivery — “it’s marketing and speed in one.” So far the drone has delivered one box and crashed into a pond.
The cloud provider holding all your data announces it’s leaving the market in 30 days. Migration usually takes six months.
right: Find a buyer for the provider

text: Quality found that besides the defective batch, there are two more “suspicious” ones. Recalling all three triples the reputational hit.
IT proposes shutting off all external access to every system for a week while they hunt for the vulnerability. Remote workers are outraged.
The bank froze the company’s accounts “pending clarification” over a suspiciously large refund to customers after the recall.
The data protection lawyer finds that customers gave consent via a pre-checked box. The consequences are unpleasant.
In the newsletter thread, staff ask whether there’ll be layoffs because of the crisis. You don’t know yet. The board asks you to “hold off.”
The plant manager proposes stripping down the whole line over the weekend to find the defect’s source. Staff would get double pay.
Procurement wants a six-month stockpile of raw materials “for the next crisis.” The warehouse will be packed, cash frozen.
The emergency team asks who’ll talk to customers: “We need someone people trust.” Everyone looks at you.
A courier service lost 300 parcels. Its director offers a month of free deliveries as compensation. The parcels were never found.
The security auditor shows that the accounting system password is “Accounting1.” Accounting is offended it was revealed publicly.
The night duty officer sends a video: the warehouse roof is leaking right over a pallet of sugar. He’s already catching drips with buckets. Go?
The chief engineer can fix the system by morning but needs the website off all night. Nights bring 20% of your sales.
The CFO brings an evening estimate: compensating affected customers will eat the year’s company party budget. Staff don’t know about the party yet.
The CEO of another company that had a similar crisis offers to meet tonight and tell you “what definitely not to do.”
Your sister calls in the evening: “I’m at the store, and your recalled product is still on the shelf. Want me to take a photo?” It’s a big chain.
The on-duty admin reports the servers are under attack, but he’s “sort of handling it.” He’s been up for three days straight.
At 11 p.m. the crisis team suggests a final call “to sync up.” Everyone is already synced and dreaming of sleep.
At midnight a supplier writes that they did find a truck for the urgent delivery. They need your signature on the request or the truck goes elsewhere.
Your child’s school recital is tonight, and half an hour in, there’s a board call about the leak. The recital lasts 45 minutes.
The warehouse guard reports a competitor’s car came at night and photographed your trucks. He says it’s the third time.
At 11 p.m. your inner voice suggests rereading all of today’s customer complaints “to feel their pain.” There are 4,000.
Tech support says the system is restored, but every user’s password has been reset. Customers will get an email at 3 a.m.
The board chair calls late to say investors are asking whether it’s time to “change captains.” The question is sort of rhetorical.
The contractor building your new warehouse says the schedule slips by a year because they “found dinosaur bones.” It’s true.
Your partner is tired of watching you refresh the news about your crisis till midnight and hides your phone in the freezer.
10:15 p.m. The press secretary sends a list of 40 questions you may get at tomorrow’s briefing. Question 38: “Do you actually use your own product?”
A journalist who wrote hit pieces about you all year asks for help with a comment for his thesis. Help him?
A board member calls at 11 p.m. and spends half an hour describing how he handled journalists back in the nineties. Priceless advice, but you’re nodding off.
The cat knocked your printed conference speech off the desk and sat on it. The other copy is at the office. The home printer is out of ink.
The crisis team proposes staying at the office all night “in case of new stories.” Everyone wants to stay — but only if you do.
A journalist calls in the evening: “I know you’re announcing the recall tomorrow. Give me an exclusive?” The announcement is strictly confidential.
Your assistant sends tomorrow’s schedule: 6 interviews, 2 broadcasts, 1 court hearing, and “lunch with an investor on the go.” Move anything?
The podcast host sends the edit before release. Your line “We’re not afraid of mistakes” is followed immediately by the sound of breaking glass.
A supplier sends an evening photo: your cargo is neatly packed — on a dock in the wrong country. The ship sailed the other way.
After hours an employee drops by to say he warned about this exact problem a year ago. And he has the email to prove it.
Marketing sends an evening idea: sell the recalled product as a “limited edition of mistakes.” Legal is against it; sales is for it.
At an industry association banquet, someone asks if it’s true a competitor is buying your company. The rumors have been going for a week.
At night, your inner voice comes up with the perfect answer to a tricky question a journalist asked you three days ago. Write it down?
left: Write it down and learn it

text: The parking attendant says a photographer has been standing by your car all evening. Yours is the last car in the lot.
A TV channel invites you to a late-night show at 11 p.m.: “CEOs Answer.” Small audience, but very lively.
The auditors are working late and ask where they can dine on the company’s tab. It’s the second time they’ve hinted at a pricey restaurant.
The board chair wants a list by morning of everyone “responsible for the crisis.” The list is essentially the whole team, plus you.
After a tough day, the leadership team suggests going to a sauna together “for team bonding.” You have court in the morning.
In the evening, your lawyer sends a one-word message: “Found it.” An hour later — silence. Calls don’t go through.
A neighbor recognized you from TV and comes by in the evening with a complaint about your product, holding a three-year-old receipt.
During an evening video call with foreign shareholders, the interpreter drops out. All that’s left is your English and their patience.
A business school invites you to teach an evening masterclass: “Crisis Management.” Your crisis is still ongoing. Students will ask about it.
After the evening board meeting, a director asks for a ride home. It’s your chance for a heart-to-heart — or to hear criticism.
In the evening, the PR director admits to thinking about quitting: “Too many crises for one year.” The crises aren’t your fault, but...
The company newsletter with your letter to staff goes out in the evening. A minute later you spot a typo in the greeting: “Dear colleages.”
A former employee writes in the evening that journalists are offering him money for “inside info.” He asks how much you’ll offer to keep him quiet.
Your college-age son says his university is studying your company as a case called “How Not to Do It.” He got an A for his presentation.
The CEO of a major client invites you to dinner at his country house to “discuss your crisis in a relaxed setting.” It’s a two-hour drive.
10 p.m. A courier delivers a huge bouquet from a competitor with a card: “Hang in there, colleagues. We’re with you.” Very big and suspiciously sincere.
Call center staff organized a “support wall” of notes to customers on their own. One note reads: “We’re shocked too.”
7:30 a.m. The communications director suggests starting every day with a “press warm-up”: five minutes answering imaginary awkward questions. Start?
The trade show organizer says your booth was mistakenly placed next to the company you’re suing. Opening is in an hour.
Investors want a morning call before the market opens to “calm the market.” You haven’t calmed down yourself yet.
HR proposes sending everyone a guide, “How Not to Talk to Journalists.” It’s 12 pages and reads like a spy manual.
The press office wants your website photo changed: in the current one you “smile too much for a crisis.” The photographer arrives in an hour.
On the morning call with the regions, a branch director asks why he learned about the problem from the news. Silence falls.
First thing, your assistant brings printouts of all overnight news about the company. The stack is thicker than the morning paper. Read it before the meeting?
The risk director brings the annual risk map. The biggest risk is labeled “The Unexpected.” He proposes a separate budget for the unexpected.
The lab needs a decision this morning: publish test results that came out worse than expected? Competitors don’t publish their bad results.
Your courier service is on strike. Orders are piling up. Office staff offer to deliver the most urgent ones in their own cars.
The sales director calls from the airport: the best client canceled the meeting after the leak news. Should he still fly?
right: Bring him back to the office

text: A forum moderator asks you to record a morning video greeting for attendees. You record it in the car at a red light, and people start honking behind you.
Reception reports two film crews, a courier with flowers, and an inspector are here to see you. All at once, all for “literally a minute.”
The board demands daily reputation reports with a “mood index” in percent. No such index exists.
IT security found that staff forward work files to personal email “to work from home.” 12,000 such emails in a month.
A longtime partner calls in the morning and carefully says he’s pausing the joint project “for a while”: “I don’t want to end up in your headlines.”
Staff showed up this morning in “We Stand With the Company!” T-shirts to support the brand. The shirts have a crooked logo.
The press attaché suggests “warming up” journalists in the morning: you personally make them coffee at the office. That’s 15 journalists and one temperamental coffee machine.
The compliance officer announces that your conference speech last year violates company policy. The policy was written after the speech.
An international partner sends a six-page letter demanding “transparency” after the scandal. The reply must be in English by evening.
At a conference, it turns out you and your main competitor have identical “Our Values” slides. Yours is shown second.
The media trainer films you, then shows you adjusting your glasses 47 times during the interview. He wants three more sessions.
Business lunch with an editor-in-chief. He orders the most expensive dish and says: “So, tell me what’s really going on.”
Communications wants to launch an internal podcast where you answer staff questions weekly. First question: “Are we getting a raise?”
The regulator invites you to a meeting on new data protection rules. You’ll speak in front of every competitor — and after the leak, they’ll ask you first.
The plant director asks permission to keep journalists out of the factory “until the crisis ends.” Journalists are already writing that you’re hiding something.
The industry association invites you to be its chair. An honor, but it means meetings every Wednesday and forever being the “voice of the industry” in the press.
Legal warns: anything you say publicly could become evidence in court. You’re speaking at a conference in an hour.
The brand manager shows the new post-rebrand logo. It looks suspiciously like the old one, rotated 3 degrees. It cost as much as an apartment.
right: Send it back to the agency

text: A saleswoman accidentally ended up in a news segment talking about the company. Everyone’s praising her, and her boss is sulking he wasn’t asked.
Support asks permission to talk to customers “like humans” instead of following the script. Legal approved the script; nobody approved humanity.
The strategy director proposes a “public roadmap of fixes,” updated weekly. If we miss a deadline, everyone will see.
A journalist offers you a monthly column in his publication. The fee is symbolic, the readers are the whole market, the deadline is always yesterday.
Logistics reports the trucks carrying the recalled batch accidentally delivered it back to the stores instead of the warehouse.
A security officer offers to find out which employees talked to journalists. His methods are “perfectly legal, but unpleasant.”
Live on air, the forum host asks you and your rival’s CEO to shake hands “as a sign of industry peace.” You’re suing him.
Over lunch, the CFO says the crisis has already cost the company the price of a new office. He asks you to sign a 15% spending cut.
In a meeting, the marketing director suggests “blending in” and keeping heads down until the storm passes. The product director wants to “go on the attack.”
Your secretary says a journalist called asking if it’s true your office is bigger than a school gym and has its own fountain.
In the evening, the board chair praises how you handled the press conference and suggests “building on the success” with three more broadcasts this week.
At the evening company party, the host announces a contest: “Who does the best CEO-at-a-press-conference impression?” Staff are already lining up.
Legal reminds you in the evening: the appeal deadline is tomorrow. The text is 90% done but needs your signature and “a couple of paragraphs from the heart.”
At 9 p.m. the IT director proposes updating all systems “while nobody’s working.” Last time, exactly that kind of update caused the outage.
A blogger who slammed you all week posts a video apology in the evening: “I was wrong, they’re okay.” Commenters now want an apology from you.
Your navigation app routes you to the morning regulator meeting through a courtyard where a TV crew is filming complaints about your company. The detour adds twenty minutes.
Before an important speech, your coach advises eating a banana and “talking to the hall while it’s empty.” The cleaner eyes you with concern.
The press office wakes you with a call: overnight, a draft report was accidentally published on the website with “NOT FOR PUBLICATION” in every paragraph.
The corporate video cameraman arrived at 7 a.m. to film “a leader’s morning.” He wants shots of you jogging in the park. You don’t jog.
The trucking company says drivers refuse to come to your warehouse: the access road was washed out by rain. Today’s shipments are at risk.
A board member sends a morning link to “10 Mistakes Leaders Make in a Crisis” and writes: “Find at least three in yourself.”
At 7:40 a.m. a PR staffer whispers that journalists dug up your school report card overnight. You got a C in spelling. Tomorrow: an article on your literacy.
The plant manager asks you to approve a “silence plan”: no smoke breaks by the fence where journalists are camped. The smokers protest.
The CTO wants to publish a detailed outage post-mortem with code and diagrams. Engineers praise the openness; security is tearing its hair out.
The morning panel moderator asks each participant to describe a failure that taught them a lot. Your latest failure is still in the news.
A consumer association published a packaging ranking this morning. Yours won “Hardest-to-Open Box of the Year.”
A distributor calls at 8 a.m.: his warehouse flooded and all your products are floating. He suggests “discussing who’s to blame.”
The press secretary asks you not to wear the red tie on air: “In a crisis, red looks aggressive.” Your other ties are at the dry cleaner.
Procurement reports the plastic supplier is discontinuing your bottles due to new regulations. Switching to glass doubles truck weight.
The IT director shows you: 40,000 hacking attempts overnight, all failed. He wants a bonus for the team “for nothing happening.”
The morning paper calls you “the industry’s most silent CEO.” The press office thinks it’s time to speak. You think silence is a tactic.
A recruitment agency offers to “refresh” your team after the crisis by replacing two directors with “more media-friendly faces.” The candidates’ portfolios are all TV appearances.
The morning show host asks: “Would you buy your own product?” You genuinely think about it, and the live-air pause lasts four seconds.
The regulator invites you to volunteer as a “pilot company” for the new rules. Honor, attention, and endless inspections in one package.
At a conference, the host asks all panelists for a group selfie. You end up between two people you’re suing.
The advertising lawyer bans the words “best,” “most,” and “delicious” from the new commercial. That leaves “decent.” Marketing is sobbing.
A crisis comms consultant suggests changing your message tone daily: Monday — empathy, Tuesday — resolve, Wednesday — humor.
A trade journal wants to interview you together with your long-retired mentor. He loves telling stories about your rookie mistakes.
The board asks you to explain to shareholders why the PR budget tripled while reputation halved.
The packing floor reports the new batch’s label says “Madewithlove” with no spaces. The batch is 200,000 units.
At a meeting, a regulator casually praises your competitor for “exemplary disclosure.” Everyone looks at you.
The press office used a stock photo in a release — and it turned out to be your own former employee, who’s suing the company.
At the shareholder meeting, an elderly shareholder spends half an hour describing how your product “tasted better thirty years ago.” The hall applauds.
Training proposes a “Crisis Communications” course for all managers. It’s taught by the person who consulted on your crisis last year.
An employee offers to write a song supporting the company and post it online. Turns out he has 200,000 followers.
The external auditor finds your “eco-friendly” warehouse is heated by a diesel generator nobody has turned off since last winter.
At a conference, your own five-year-old forecast slide is shown as an example of “the industry’s boldest failed predictions.”
The board chair invites you fishing to “talk about the future.” The trip starts at 4 a.m. You’ve never held a fishing rod.
At 10:40 p.m., a news site’s night editor asks you to confirm you’re leaving the company. You’re sitting in your office, going nowhere.
At an evening reception, your partner’s wife loudly asks if it’s true you “fired someone over a social media post.” Conversations around you go quiet.
Your inner voice notes it’s the fifth night in a row you’ve promised yourself to leave early. It’s 9:30 p.m., with 40 unread emails.
On an evening video call with the board, your kid walks behind you in pajamas and waves. The chair waves back.
At 8 p.m. a supplier proposes settling the quality dispute simply: “Let’s each admit half the blame.” The lawyers have gone home.
The corporate lawyer admits he missed the deadline to respond to a claim and suggests “changing the date on the envelope.” Pretend you didn’t hear?
left: Forbid it and deal with it

text: An evening comedy show host parodies you on air. It’s a good parody: staff are laughing, and the board demands you “take action.”
In the evening, the marketing director suggests an emergency switch of ad agencies. The current one came up with the slogan everyone’s parodying.
Security reports staff showed up at the office at 9 p.m. with a cake: “Happy company birthday!” You forgot it’s the anniversary.
left: Go out and cut the cake

text: Before leaving, your secretary asks whether to answer a journalist’s email sent “yesterday at 11:59 p.m.” demanding a response “by midnight.”
The head of support asks you to come in for the morning shift and work the phones “for morale.” The shift starts at 6 a.m.
Over evening tea, a lawyer friend looks over the suit against you for free and says: “In their shoes, I’d have sued too.” The tea goes cold.
In the evening an employee confesses he’s the one who accidentally posted the typo that started the scandal. He’s ready to resign.
The PR director sends an evening report: a thousand stories about the company this month, seven of them positive. He suggests celebrating “seven victories.”
You’re at the airport in the evening; your conference flight is delayed. A journalist you’ve been dodging for a month sits down next to you. He recognizes you.
Late in the evening the board chair writes: “Great work on this crisis. By the way, we have another one.” And attaches a link.
At dinner, the family sets a rule: no talk of work, journalists, or courts. Three minutes later you’re talking about the court case.
Friday evening. Your inner voice suggests a weekly recap: two broadcasts, one inspection, an outage, a lawsuit, and three memes. You survived. How will you celebrate?
